triage.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
triage.reason: Megaloblastic anemia with neuropathy; diagnosis reachable from diet, medication and surgical history plus labs.

review_issues: presentation: term 'Gait disturbance' not found in SNOMED CT
presentation: term 'Gait disturbance' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Vibration sense impaired' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Pinprick sensation impaired' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Strict vegans and vegetarians are at higher risk
More common in people who have had gastric or ileal surgery
More common in people with autoimmune gastritis or pernicious anemia

risk_factors.text: Strict vegan or vegetarian diet without supplementation
Pernicious anemia or autoimmune atrophic gastritis
Prior gastric or ileal resection or bariatric surgery
Long-term proton pump inhibitor or histamine H2 blocker use
Crohn disease, celiac disease or other malabsorptive conditions

family_history: Pernicious anemia in a first-degree relative
social_history: Food insecurity or limited access to animal products

chief_complaints.text: I feel tired all the time
My hands and feet feel numb and tingly
I've been short of breath walking up stairs
I keep forgetting things and feel foggy
My tongue is sore and smooth

hpi.duration: Weeks to years; frequently present for many months before diagnosis
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea, with or without numbness and tingling in the hands and feet; neurologic symptoms may progress even when anemia is mild
hpi.location: Generalized; neurologic symptoms are symmetric and distal in the hands and feet
hpi.quality: Tiredness and weakness; numbness, tingling or a 'pins and needles' feeling in the extremities; unsteady walking in more advanced cases
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate at first, worsening over time; neurologic deficits can become disabling
aggravating: Walking or standing for long periods

associated_symptoms.text: Numbness and tingling in the hands and feet

pertinent_negatives: Blood in stool or black stools

positives.text: Numbness and tingling in hands and feet

atypical.how_it_differs: May present mainly with cognitive decline, balance problems or falls rather than anemia; neurologic signs can dominate.
Infants and children may present with failure to thrive, developmental delay or irritability; strict vegan mothers can lead to deficiency in breastfed infants.
Symptoms may be attributed to pregnancy; deficiency can cause fatigue and anemia that do not respond to iron.
Not a typical modifier for this condition; pernicious anemia is autoimmune and may coexist with other autoimmune diseases.

general.moderate: Pale and tired-appearing, able to ambulate but fatigued
general.severe: Markedly pale, weak, short of breath with minimal exertion
general.critical: Ill-appearing, pale, tachycardic, may be confused or unsteady

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctivae, palms and skin in good lighting
Inspect the tongue and oral mucosa
findings.finding: Smooth, red, beefy tongue with loss of papillae

findings.maneuver: Inspect the corners of the mouth
findings.finding: Fissuring and erythema at the oral commissures

findings.maneuver: Inspect the sclerae
Auscultate the heart at the apex and base
findings.finding: Soft systolic flow murmur from increased cardiac output

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein at 45 degrees
Auscultate the lung bases
Press the dorsum of each foot for several seconds
Place a vibrating 128 Hz tuning fork on the great toe and compare with the wrist
findings.finding: Reduced or absent vibration sense in the feet, symmetric and distal

findings.maneuver: Move the great toe up and down with the patient's eyes closed and ask the direction
findings.finding: Impaired joint position sense in the toes

findings.maneuver: Test pinprick sensation on the distal lower extremities and compare with the thigh
findings.finding: Reduced pinprick sensation in a symmetric stocking distribution

findings.maneuver: Test light touch with a cotton wisp on the feet and hands
Ask the patient to stand with feet together and eyes closed
findings.finding: Increased sway or falls with eyes closed (sensory ataxia)

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient walking heel-to-toe
Stroke the lateral sole of the foot from heel to base of the great toe
Test the knee and ankle reflexes with a reflex hammer
Test the knee and ankle reflexes with a reflex hammer
Test dorsiflexion and plantar flexion against resistance
Assess orientation, attention and short-term recall
findings.finding: Slowed processing, impaired recall or disorientation

findings.maneuver: Ask about mood and anhedonia
Palpate the liver edge and splenic tip
Palpate the cervical, axillary and inguinal lymph node basins

labs.caveat: Anemia may be absent in early or purely neurologic deficiency; hemoglobin falls as the deficiency progresses.
Macrocytosis can precede anemia; a normal MCV does not exclude the diagnosis, especially if iron deficiency coexists.
Low or inappropriately normal for the degree of anemia, indicating a hypoproliferative marrow.
Mild thrombocytopenia from ineffective hematopoiesis; severe thrombocytopenia should prompt another explanation.
Mild leukopenia with hypersegmented neutrophils; marked leukocytosis or blasts suggests another diagnosis.
Elevated from intramedullary destruction of red cell precursors; nonspecific.
Mild indirect hyperbilirubinemia from ineffective erythropoiesis; marked jaundice is unusual.
Levels between 200 and 300 pg/mL are borderline; methylmalonic acid and homocysteine help when clinical suspicion is high.
Normal. Checked to separate B12 deficiency from folate deficiency, which causes identical megaloblastic anemia.
Normal. Hypothyroidism is a common cause of macrocytic anemia and must be excluded.
May rise mildly with dehydration or concurrent kidney disease; not a direct marker of B12 deficiency.

findings.finding: Nonspecific ST-T wave changes from anemia

imaging.study: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with small bowel biopsy
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pernicious anemia, atrophic gastritis or malabsorption

findings.text: Atrophic gastric mucosa with loss of folds
Small bowel mucosal atrophy with blunted villi

imaging.study: MRI of the spinal cord without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Myelopathy or unexplained upper motor neuron signs

findings.text: T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns of the cervical or thoracic cord (subacute combined degeneration)

initial.why: Shows macrocytic anemia, high RDW and possible cytopenias
Excludes folate deficiency, which causes identical megaloblastic anemia
Hypothyroidism is a common cause of macrocytic anemia
Assesses LDH, bilirubin and albumin as markers of ineffective erythropoiesis and overall status
Baseline electrolytes and kidney function before treatment

supporting.why: Elevated in B12 deficiency but not folate deficiency; helps when B12 is borderline
supporting.only_if: serum B12 is borderline (200–300 pg/mL) or clinical suspicion remains high

supporting.why: Elevated in both B12 and folate deficiency; supports the diagnosis when B12 is borderline
supporting.only_if: serum B12 is borderline or folate results are unclear

supporting.why: Supports pernicious anemia as the cause

supporting.test: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with small bowel biopsy
supporting.only_if: malabsorption or pernicious anemia is suspected

supporting.test: MRI of the spinal cord without contrast
supporting.only_if: myelopathy or upper motor neuron signs are present

not_indicated.why: No role in the evaluation of anemia or neuropathy
Not needed unless pancreatic insufficiency is suspected
Does not evaluate vitamin B12 deficiency or its causes

decision_points: Check methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when serum B12 is borderline (200–300 pg/mL) and suspicion is high
Treat with intramuscular or high-dose oral B12; do not give folate alone because it can worsen neurologic injury
Look for the underlying cause (diet, metformin, PPI, pernicious anemia, malabsorption) once deficiency is confirmed

differential.name: Folate deficiency
differential.why_considered: Causes an identical megaloblastic anemia with macrocytosis, fatigue and glossitis; often coexists with B12 deficiency.
differential.trigger: Megaloblastic anemia with a normal or borderline B12 level, or alcohol use, poor diet or pregnancy.

history: Poor diet, alcohol use disorder or pregnancy
exam: Pallor and glossitis without vibration or position sense loss
No sensory ataxia or Romberg sign

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Common cause of macrocytic anemia, fatigue, cognitive slowing and cold intolerance.
differential.trigger: Macrocytosis with fatigue, weight gain, constipation or cold intolerance.

history: Weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, dry skin
exam: Dry skin, bradycardia, delayed relaxation of reflexes, goiter
No impaired vibration or position sense
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4

differential.name: Myelodysplastic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Causes macrocytic anemia with cytopenias, especially in older adults.
differential.trigger: Macrocytic anemia with leukopenia or thrombocytopenia that does not improve after B12 replacement.

history: No dietary or medication risk factors for B12 deficiency
exam: Pallor and possible petechiae or ecchymoses
labs: Normal B12, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
Bone marrow biopsy showing dysplasia or increased blasts

differential.name: Copper deficiency
differential.why_considered: Rare but causes a myeloneuropathy with sensory ataxia and spastic gait that mimics subacute combined degeneration.

history: Prior gastric or bariatric surgery, zinc overload or malabsorption
labs: Normal B12, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
imaging: T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns on spinal MRI

differential.name: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Common cause of symmetric distal numbness and tingling in the feet.

history: Painful burning feet, worse at night
exam: Stocking-distribution sensory loss with reduced ankle reflexes
labs: Normal B12, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine

differential.name: Alcohol use disorder
differential.why_considered: Causes macrocytic anemia, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive impairment and poor nutrition.

exam: Signs of chronic liver disease, tremor, ataxia
labs: Elevated AST/ALT ratio, GGT and MCV

differential.name: Multiple myeloma
differential.why_considered: Can cause anemia, fatigue and neurologic symptoms from hypercalcemia or cord compression.

exam: Pallor, bone tenderness, possible cord compression signs
labs: Elevated total protein with low albumin, elevated calcium and creatinine
Monoclonal protein on serum protein electrophoresis
imaging: Lytic bone lesions on skeletal survey or MRI

differential.name: Medication-induced macrocytosis
differential.why_considered: Hydroxyurea, methotrexate, zidovudine and some antiepileptics cause macrocytosis without true B12 deficiency.

history: Current use of a known macrocytosis-causing medication
No dietary or malabsorptive risk factors
labs: Normal B12, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
Macrocytosis resolves after stopping the drug

severity.mild: Borderline low B12 with mild macrocytosis or no anemia; fatigue and subtle paresthesia; no gait or cognitive impairment.
severity.moderate: Megaloblastic anemia with hemoglobin 8–10.5 g/dL, clear paresthesia, impaired vibration sense and possible glossitis.
severity.severe: Marked anemia with hemoglobin 6–8 g/dL, sensory ataxia, Romberg sign, cognitive slowing and difficulty with daily activities.
severity.critical: Profound anemia with hemoglobin below 6 g/dL, tachycardia, dyspnea at rest, confusion or syncope; may require urgent transfusion and inpatient care.

red_flags.finding: New confusion, disorientation or memory loss
red_flags.meaning: Severe neurologic involvement; needs urgent evaluation and treatment

red_flags.finding: Unsteady gait, frequent falls or inability to walk heel-to-toe
red_flags.meaning: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord; treat promptly to prevent permanent damage

red_flags.finding: Hemoglobin below 6 g/dL or symptomatic anemia at rest
red_flags.meaning: Severe anemia; consider transfusion and inpatient monitoring

red_flags.finding: Heart rate over 120 beats per minute or hypotension
New focal weakness, bowel or bladder dysfunction
red_flags.meaning: Possible cord compression or another structural lesion; image urgently

complications.name: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
clues: Symmetric paresthesia and impaired vibration or position sense
T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns on spinal MRI

complications.name: Permanent peripheral neuropathy
clues: Numbness and tingling that persist after B12 levels normalize
Reduced ankle reflexes and distal sensory loss

complications.name: Cognitive impairment and dementia
clues: Progressive memory loss and slowed processing
Improvement or stabilization after B12 replacement

complications.name: Gastric or colorectal cancer associated with pernicious anemia
clues: Iron deficiency, weight loss or gastrointestinal bleeding

special_populations.differences: May present with cognitive decline, balance problems or falls rather than anemia; pernicious anemia is more common and neurologic signs can dominate.
Infants and children may present with failure to thrive, developmental delay or irritability; breastfed infants of strict vegan mothers are at risk.
Fatigue and anemia may be attributed to pregnancy; deficiency can cause anemia that does not respond to iron and may affect the fetus.
Anemia may be multifactorial; B12 deficiency should still be considered and treated if confirmed.
Long-term metformin use increases risk; neuropathy may be attributed to diabetes rather than B12 deficiency.

key_questions.question: What do you eat in a typical day, and do you eat meat, fish, eggs or dairy?
key_questions.looking_for: Strict vegan or vegetarian diet without supplementation, or a very limited diet; vitamin B12 comes only from animal products and fortified foods

key_questions.question: Do you take any vitamins or supplements, and do any of them contain B12?
key_questions.looking_for: No B12-containing supplement despite a restricted diet

key_questions.question: Have you ever had stomach or intestinal surgery, including weight-loss surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Gastric or ileal resection, gastric bypass or other bariatric surgery, which impairs B12 absorption

key_questions.question: Do you take metformin, or a proton pump inhibitor or acid reducer regularly?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-term metformin, omeprazole, pantoprazole, ranitidine or famotidine use

key_questions.question: Do you have any condition that affects how you absorb food, like Crohn disease, celiac disease or chronic pancreatitis?
key_questions.looking_for: Malabsorptive conditions that reduce B12 absorption

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had pernicious anemia or another autoimmune disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Pernicious anemia or autoimmune disease in a first-degree relative

key_questions.question: Do you have any numbness, tingling or a pins-and-needles feeling in your hands or feet?
key_questions.looking_for: Symmetric, distal paresthesia suggesting neurologic involvement

key_questions.question: Have you noticed trouble with your balance or walking, or do you feel unsteady in the dark?
key_questions.looking_for: Sensory ataxia or unsteady gait from subacute combined degeneration

key_questions.question: Have you been more forgetful, foggy or irritable than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Cognitive slowing, memory problems or mood change

key_questions.question: Is your tongue sore, smooth or red, or have you had mouth sores?
Have you had any heavy periods, blood in your stool or black stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Another source of blood loss that could explain anemia and change the workup

key_questions.question: Do you use nitrous oxide, sometimes called laughing gas or whippets?
key_questions.looking_for: Recreational or repeated nitrous oxide exposure, which inactivates B12 and can cause myeloneuropathy

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Alcohol use disorder, which causes poor nutrition and macrocytic anemia

key_questions.question: Do you have any other autoimmune conditions, like thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes or vitiligo?
key_questions.looking_for: Autoimmune disease that clusters with pernicious anemia

reasoning_points: Gradual fatigue, exertional dyspnea and pallor from a macrocytic anemia
Symmetric distal paresthesia with impaired vibration and position sense, and possible sensory ataxia, indicating neurologic involvement
A risk factor for low B12: strict vegan or vegetarian diet, gastric or ileal surgery, pernicious anemia, metformin or long-term acid suppression, or malabsorption
Macrocytosis with a high RDW and a low reticulocyte count for the degree of anemia
Low serum vitamin B12, with normal folate and normal TSH
Elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when the B12 level is borderline
Folate deficiency excluded, because it causes an identical megaloblastic anemia but a normal methylmalonic acid
The underlying cause identified so that the right replacement route and monitoring are chosen

easy: Older adult with fatigue, pallor and a smooth sore tongue
Strict vegan for years with no supplement
Macrocytic anemia with a low serum B12
Numbness and tingling in the feet with reduced vibration sense
medium: Long-term metformin or proton pump inhibitor use with mild macrocytosis
Borderline B12 level (200–300 pg/mL) requiring methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
Anemia with coexisting iron deficiency, so the MCV is normal
Neurologic symptoms with little or no anemia
hard: Older adult presenting mainly with cognitive decline or falls rather than anemia
Pernicious anemia with a normal-looking diet and no gastrointestinal symptoms
Myelopathy with spastic gait and dorsal column signs mimicking copper deficiency
Breastfed infant of a strict vegan mother with failure to thrive and developmental delay
Macrocytosis that does not improve after B12 replacement, suggesting myelodysplastic syndrome
